title: Nasreddin Hodja: Seven Short Tales
source: Traditional tales of Nasreddin Hodja, told from Turkey to India for 700 years. Retold for this tool; one early English collection is George Borrow's "The Turkish Jester" (1884).

chapters.title: Do You Know What I'm Going to Say?
chapters.text: One Friday the Hodja climbed into the pulpit and asked, "Do you know what I am going to say to you?" "No," said the people. "Then what is the use of telling people who know nothing?" he said, and went home. Next Friday he asked again. This time they said, "Yes, we know." "Then you don't need me to tell you," he said, and went home. The third Friday the people had a plan. When he asked, half of them shouted "Yes!" and half shouted "No!" The Hodja smiled. "Wonderful," he said. "Then let the half who know tell the half who don't." And he went home.

chapters.title: Eat, My Coat, Eat!
chapters.text: The Hodja went to a rich man's feast straight from his field, in his old working clothes. Nobody greeted him, nobody gave him a seat, and the food never came his way. So he walked home, put on his best fur coat and came back. Now the host bowed, sat him at the head of the table and placed the finest soup in front of him. The Hodja dipped the sleeve of his coat into the bowl. "Eat, my coat, eat!" he said. The guests stared. "Well," said the Hodja, "it was the coat you invited, not me. So the coat should have the dinner."

chapters.title: The Cauldron That Had a Baby
chapters.text: The Hodja borrowed a big copper cauldron from his neighbour. When he gave it back, there was a small pot inside it. "What's this?" asked the neighbour. "Good news," said the Hodja. "While it was with me, your cauldron gave birth." The neighbour was delighted and took both. A month later the Hodja borrowed the cauldron again, and this time he did not bring it back. At last the neighbour knocked on his door. "Where is my cauldron?" The Hodja looked very sad. "I'm sorry. Your cauldron has died." "Died? A cauldron can't die!" said the neighbour. "Strange," said the Hodja. "You believed it could have a baby."

chapters.title: The Ring Under the Streetlamp
chapters.text: One evening a friend found the Hodja on his knees in the street, searching the ground under a lamp. "What have you lost?" "My ring," said the Hodja. The friend got down and helped him search. After a long time with no luck, the friend asked, "Are you sure you dropped it here?" "Oh no," said the Hodja. "I dropped it inside my house." "Then why are we looking out here?" "Because," said the Hodja, "there is much more light out here."

chapters.title: Riding Backwards
chapters.text: The Hodja set off for the mosque one morning with his students walking behind him. To everyone's surprise, he was sitting on his donkey facing its tail. "Hodja, you're riding backwards!" they said. "Think about it," he replied. "If I sat the normal way, my back would be to you, and that would be rude. If you walked in front of me, your backs would be to me, and that would be rude too. This way we can all see each other and nobody is rude. Only the donkey cannot see where we are going, and he knows the way better than all of us."

chapters.title: The Smell of the Soup
chapters.text: A poor man sat outside a cook-shop eating dry bread, holding it in the steam of the shop's soup so it would smell nice. The cook ran out and grabbed him. "You enjoyed the smell of my soup. Pay for it!" They went to the Hodja, who was the judge that day. The Hodja listened, took a few coins out of his own pocket and shook them next to the cook's ear. Jingle, jingle. "Did you hear that?" he asked. "Yes," said the cook. "Good," said the Hodja, and put the coins back in his pocket. "The smell of the soup is paid for with the sound of the money. Case closed."

chapters.title: Whom Do You Believe?
chapters.text: A neighbour came to borrow the Hodja's donkey. The Hodja didn't want to lend it, so he said, "I'm sorry, the donkey isn't here today." Just then, from the stable behind the house, the donkey began to bray loudly: hee-haw, hee-haw! "Hodja!" said the neighbour. "You said it wasn't here, but I can hear it!" The Hodja drew himself up, very offended. "Shame on you," he said. "I have a white beard and I am a respected man, and you believe a donkey instead of me?"

title: Andare, the King's Jester
source: Traditional Sri Lankan folk tales of Andare, said to be jester at the court of a Kandyan king in the 1700s. The details vary from teller to teller. Retold for this tool.

chapters.title: Behave Like an Ox
chapters.text: When Andare was a boy, his mother took him to a wedding. On the way she warned him: "Be good. Behave like an ox," which in the village way of speaking means: be quiet and well-behaved. At the wedding the guests sat down to eat. Andare did not. He got down on all fours, went round the hall saying "Moo!", and started eating the decorations of banana leaves and grass. His mother nearly fainted. "What are you doing?" "Exactly what you told me," said Andare, chewing. "An ox." It was the last time she ever gave him advice with a picture in it.

chapters.title: The King's Sugar
chapters.text: One day Andare saw a mat of sugar drying in the palace courtyard and wanted some badly. The king saw him looking and teased him: "That is only white sand, Andare." Andare threw himself onto the mat, crying, "My life is too hard! I want to die! I'll eat this sand and end it all!", and stuffed himself with handfuls of "sand". The king laughed so much he let him go on. Later the king sighed and said, "Your poor wife will miss you. Take some of the sand home to her too." Andare didn't need to be told twice: he went home with a full bag. In some versions he went even further, but that is another story.

chapters.title: Moving the Hill
chapters.text: A farmer had a huge rock in the middle of his field and could not plough around it. "I'll throw it away for you," said Andare, "but only if you feed me rice and chicken curry every day for three months, to build up my strength." The farmer agreed. Andare ate very well for three months. On the big day the whole village came to watch. Andare rolled up his sleeves, bent down next to the rock and said: "Right. Now lift it up and put it on my shoulder, and I'll throw it." Nobody could lift it, of course. "Then it is not my fault," said Andare, and went home, well fed.

chapters.title: The Golden Mango
chapters.text: In the king's garden grew one special tree of golden mangoes, and nobody was allowed to touch them. One day the guards caught Andare with a golden mango in his hand. He was taken before the king. "Why did you steal my royal mango?" asked the king. "Your Majesty, I didn't steal it," said Andare. "I was testing it. If it truly is a royal mango, it should be fit for a king. Someone had to make sure, for your safety." The king laughed so hard that, instead of punishing him, he told Andare to eat as many mangoes as he liked.

chapters.title: The Eggs in the Pond
chapters.text: The king wanted to make a fool of Andare. He secretly gave each of his ministers an egg and told them all to bathe with him in the royal pond. "Let's see who can dive down and bring up an egg," he said. One by one the ministers dived and came up holding an egg. Then it was Andare's turn. He dived, came up with nothing, flapped his arms and crowed, "Cock-a-doodle-doo!" "What's that for?" asked the king. "Your Majesty," said Andare, "with so many hens laying eggs in this pond, surely you need at least one rooster."

chapters.title: The Minister Who Couldn't Sleep
chapters.text: A chief minister could not fall asleep at night, so he ordered Andare to come to his room and tell him stories until he did. Andare told one story, then another, then another. Every time he stopped, the minister said, "Go on." Midnight came. Andare's eyes were closing, but the minister was still wide awake and asking for more. At last Andare lost his patience and shouted: "Either this fool must go to sleep, or he must let me sleep!" The minister was so shocked that he lay quiet and, to everyone's surprise, was soon fast asleep.

chapters.title: The Last Joke
chapters.text: Andare made the court laugh all his life. When he finally died, people found him lying with his arms and legs stretched out wide, like a star. Nothing would make him lie straight, so the carpenters had to build a coffin in that same strange shape: wide and square, with corners for his hands and feet. When the king saw it, he laughed and wiped his eyes at the same time. "Even in death," he said, "Andare makes us laugh."

title: Mahadenamutta and His Five Pupils
source: Traditional Sri Lankan folk tales of Mahadenamutta, the "wise man" whose advice always goes wrong. Some scholars trace them to 18th-century Tamil tales. Retold for this tool.

chapters.title: The Great Wise Man
chapters.text: Long ago, in a village, lived Mahadenamutta, the man who knew everything. At least, that is what he said, and he said it very loudly. He had five loyal pupils, each named after the first thing people noticed about him: Pol Bae Muna, whose face was round like half a coconut; Kotu Kittaya, thin as a stick; Idikatu Paencha, thin as a needle; Rabbada Aiya, with a big round belly; and Puvak Badilla, whose belly was shaped like an arecanut. Wherever there was a problem, Mahadenamutta and his pupils arrived to solve it. And wherever they solved a problem, there was soon a bigger one.

chapters.title: Waiting for the River to Sleep
chapters.text: One night the master and his pupils came to a river they had to cross. The water was rushing and gurgling. "Stop!" said Mahadenamutta. "Listen. The river is awake. If we cross now, it will swallow us. We must wait until the river falls asleep." So they sat on the bank and waited, and waited, all night long. Some time before dawn, Pol Bae Muna dropped his burning torch into the water, and it went: SSSS! "Run!" shouted the master. "We have woken it up again!" They ran all the way home and never did get across.

chapters.title: Sowing Without Footprints
chapters.text: A farmer asked Mahadenamutta for help. "I need to sow my muddy paddy field, but whoever walks in it to scatter the seed leaves deep footprints." The master thought hard. "Simple," he said. "The sower must not walk." He put the fattest pupil, Rabbada Aiya, with the basket of seed onto a stretcher, and told the other four to carry him up and down the field while he threw the seed. The pupils carried him all day. When they finished, the field was covered with deep footprints: eight feet at a time, instead of two.

chapters.title: The Missing Pupil
chapters.text: After crossing a stream, Mahadenamutta told his pupils to count themselves to make sure nobody had drowned. The first pupil counted: "One, two, three, four." Only four! He had forgotten to count himself. The next one tried: four again. Every pupil counted, and every pupil found only four. They began to weep for their lost brother. A passing traveller asked what was wrong, then lined them up and tapped each one on the head as they called out their number: one, two, three, four, five! "A miracle!" cried the master. "Our brother has come back to us!" They thanked the traveller, and he went on his way laughing.

chapters.title: The Goat and the Pot
chapters.text: A goat pushed its head into a clay pot to eat the rice inside and got stuck. Its owner and the owner of the pot began to argue, and the whole village sent for Mahadenamutta. He arrived on an elephant, surrounded by his pupils, and studied the case for a long time. "The answer is clear," he said at last. "First, cut off the goat's head." It was done. The head was still stuck in the pot. "Now," said the master, "break the pot." The head came out. Both men had lost everything. "Another problem solved," said Mahadenamutta, and the pupils clapped.
